{"id":"062583ef-4e21-4b5c-bad3-89593a660d14","state":"COMPLETED","response":"# Referee report: Second-order obstructions for Erdős Problem #99

Independent research session · 28 October 2026 · Codex Route

Verdict: The exact Erdős #99 endpoint remains unresolved. I obtain a rigorous second-order necessary condition for every unrestricted global diameter minimizer, without assuming infinitesimal rigidity. This gives an algebraic obstruction to certain triangle-free contact frameworks and a complete constructive exclusion of nontrivial full two-direction unit-rhombic grid patches.

For multi-grain networks, I obtain a conditional hinge obstruction, but not a contradiction covering all multi-grain configurations. The missing step is a theorem ensuring that an appropriate diameter-decreasing flex exists, or that every equilibrium stress charges a contact moved by such a flex.

The distinction matters: the public problem remains listed as open, and a September 2026 preprint already develops related equilibrium-stress and rhombic-reduction techniques. Erdős Problems+1

## 2. A sharp second-order necessary condition

and

There is also a useful non-asymptotic identity. For any other unit-separated configuration Y=(yi)Y=(y_i)Y=(yi​) with squared diameter TYT_YTY​, equilibrium and normalization give

Indeed, the quadratic function

Es(Y)=∑f∈Fμf∥yi−yj∥2−∑e∈Cλe∥yi−yj∥2E_s(Y)=\sum_{f\in F}\mu_f\|y_i-y_j\|^2 -\sum_{e\in C}\lambda_e\|y_i-y_j\|^2Es​(Y)=f∈F∑​μf​∥yi​−yj​∥2−e∈C∑​λe​∥yi​−yj​∥2

## 3. A rigidity-free contact-flex obstruction

Define the vector space

V={v:re⋅ve=0(e∈C),vi=0 whenever i is a diametral endpoint}.(12)\mathcal V= \left\{ v: r_e\cdot v_e=0\ (e\in C),\ v_i=0\text{ whenever }i\text{ is a diametral endpoint} \right\}. \tag{12}V={v:re​⋅ve​=0(e∈C),vi​=0 whenever i is a diametral endpoint}.(12)

These fields preserve all unit contacts infinitesimally and fix every original diametral endpoint pointwise.

For v∈Vv\in\mathcal Vv∈V, all diameter terms of QsQ_sQs​ vanish, giving

Qs(v)=−∑e∈Cλe∥ve∥2≤0.(13)Q_s(v)=-\sum_{e\in C}\lambda_e\|v_e\|^2\leq0. \tag{13}Qs​(v)=−e∈C∑​λe​∥ve​∥2≤0.(13)

Theorem 2 now says that at least one equilibrium stress must assign zero weight to every contact actually moved by vvv.

In fact, one obtains a common stress for the whole flex space.

### Corollary 3: Adapted-stress support

There exists s∈S(P)s\in\mathcal S(P)s∈S(P) such that

λe=0\lambda_e=0λe​=0

for every contact eee moved by at least one v∈Vv\in\mathcal Vv∈V.

By (6) and (13), some stress has Qs(v)=0Q_s(v)=0Qs​(v)=0. Each summand in (13) is nonpositive, so all its nonzero displacement terms must have coefficient λe=0\lambda_e=0λe​=0. □\square□

This produces an exact, finite-dimensional contradiction test:

> If an active network has a diameter-endpoint-fixed contact flex, but no equilibrium stress can be supported entirely on contacts frozen by all such flexes, then that network cannot be a local diameter minimum.

The proof requires no rigidity assumption. It is also closely related to the adapted-stress reduction already described in the September 2026 Das preprint. Zenodo

## 4. Complete exclusion of full two-direction unit-rhombic grids

Here is an explicit geometrical contradiction, not merely a stress feasibility criterion.

### Theorem 4: Full unit-rhombic rectangular patches are not locally diameter-minimal, except the four-site unit square

Let

Pa,b,θ={iu+jv:0≤i≤a,0≤j≤b},P_{a,b,\theta} = \{i u+j v:0\leq i\leq a,\ 0\leq j\leq b\},Pa,b,θ​={iu+jv:0≤i≤a,0≤j≤b},

where a,b≥1a,b\geq1a,b≥1 are integers, ∥u∥=∥v∥=1\|u\|=\|v\|=1∥u∥=∥v∥=1, and the angle θ\thetaθ between u,vu,vu,v satisfies

π3<θ<2π3.\frac{\pi}{3}<\theta<\frac{2\pi}{3}.3π​<θ<32π​.

If (a,b)≠(1,1)(a,b)\ne(1,1)(a,b)=(1,1), this configuration is not a local minimum of the diameter among unit-separated configurations of the same cardinality.

It is triangle-free: its unit contacts are precisely the horizontal and vertical grid edges.

Proof, first case: θ≠π/2\theta\ne\pi/2θ=π/2. For an integer lattice displacement (m,n)(m,n)(m,n),

∥mu+nv∥2=m2+n2+2mncos⁡θ.\|mu+nv\|^2=m^2+n^2+2mn\cos\theta.∥mu+nv∥2=m2+n2+2mncosθ.

(Use m2+n2−∣mn∣≥1m^2+n^2-|mn|\geq1m2+n2−∣mn∣≥1, with equality among non-edge candidates only when ∣m∣=∣n∣=1|m|=|n|=1∣m∣=∣n∣=1; the strict cosine bound handles those cases.) Thus the only unit contacts are the two grid directions, and no unit triangle exists.

By convexity of the squared norm in the index-difference rectangle, the diameter is attained at a pair of opposite corners:

D2=a2+b2+2ab∣cos⁡θ∣.(14)D^2=a^2+b^2+2ab|\cos\theta|. \tag{14}D2=a2+b2+2ab∣cosθ∣.(14)

Move θ\thetaθ slightly toward π/2\pi/2π/2, keeping both basis-vector lengths exactly 111. This strictly decreases (14). Every unit edge remains of length 111, and every initially nonunit pair has positive slack, so by finiteness all separation constraints remain valid for sufficiently small angle changes. Hence the diameter decreases. □\square□

Proof, second case: θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2. After a rigid motion, take u=(1,0)u=(1,0)u=(1,0), v=(0,1)v=(0,1)v=(0,1). Assume a≥2a\geq2a≥2, interchanging the coordinate axes if necessary. Define

(i,j)⟼((1−ε2/2)i,j+εg(i)).(15)\boxed{ (i,j)\longmapsto \left((1-\varepsilon^2/2)i,\ j+\varepsilon g(i)\right). } \tag{15}(i,j)⟼((1−ε2/2)i,j+εg(i)).​(15)

For every horizontal adjacent pair, ∣g(i+1)−g(i)∣≥1|g(i+1)-g(i)|\geq1∣g(i+1)−g(i)∣≥1, so

∥Δp′∥2=(1−ε2/2)2+ε2[g(i+1)−g(i)]2≥1+ε44>1.(16)\begin{aligned} \|\Delta p'\|^2 &=(1-\varepsilon^2/2)^2+ \varepsilon^2[g(i+1)-g(i)]^2\\ &\geq1+\frac{\varepsilon^4}{4}>1. \end{aligned} \tag{16}∥Δp′∥2​=(1−ε2/2)2+ε2[g(i+1)−g(i)]2≥1+4ε4​>1.​(16)

All initially nonadjacent pairs have separation at least 2\sqrt22​, so they remain strictly greater than 111 for sufficiently small ε\varepsilonε. The new minimum separation is therefore 111, realized by vertical edges.

The original diameter is a2+b2\sqrt{a^2+b^2}a2+b2​, attained only by the two corner diagonals. Because g(0)=g(a)=0g(0)=g(a)=0g(0)=g(a)=0, the new squared lengths of those diagonals are both

This is an exact contradiction for a class of triangle-free networks with 4-regular interior contact graph. It also shows why merely looking for first-order improvements is insufficient: at the square grid, (15) has zero first-order change of every active contact and every diametral pair, while the diameter decreases at second order.

### Relation to the stress test

For the square grid, the velocity in (15) is

vij=(0,g(i)).v_{ij}=(0,g(i)).vij​=(0,g(i)).

Every active contact satisfies re⋅ve=0r_e\cdot v_e=0re​⋅ve​=0, and every diametral endpoint is fixed. The acceleration is aij=(−i,0)a_{ij}=(-i,0)aij​=(−i,0), and the squared-diameter variation has η=−2a2<0\eta=-2a^2<0η=−2a2<0. Conditions (8)–(9) are satisfied, giving the same contradiction through Theorem 2.

Scope restriction. The theorem applies to the entire rectangular product grid. It does not exclude a disk-cropped rhombic lattice, an irregular boundary, a variable-angle quadrilateral mesh, or a multi-grain contact network. Those are precisely the shapes for which the active diameter pattern can prevent this deformation.

## 5. Multi-grain networks: a hinge obstruction and its limitation

Assume every diametral pair is cross-grain. If there is a sign s∈{−1,1}s\in\{-1,1\}s∈{−1,1} such that every active diametral cross pair satisfies either

sfab′(0)<0,s f_{ab}'(0)<0,sfab′​(0)<0,

Proof. Set ϕ=sh\phi=shϕ=sh with h>0h>0h>0 small. Each active diametral squared distance decreases strictly: at first order in the first case, at second order in the second. Inactive pairs have strict diameter slack and remain below the original diameter by continuity. All separation constraints remain valid, as noted above. Therefore the maximum pair distance decreases strictly. □\square□

In particular, the hypothesis holds whenever every diametral cross-grain pair lies on opposite rays from the hinge site ccc: then det⁡(U,V)=0\det(U,V)=0det(U,V)=0 and U⋅V<0U\cdot V<0U⋅V<0.

This is a valid multi-grain contradiction without rigidity. It is conditional, however, on a one-site hinge and the stated diameter geometry.

### Why negative curvature alone is insufficient

Here is a triangle-free counterexample to a tempting stronger hinge argument. Let

c=(0,0),a=(1,0),b±=(−cos⁡α,±sin⁡α),α=π4,c=(0,0),\quad a=(1,0),\quad b_\pm=(-\cos\alpha,\pm\sin\alpha), \qquad \alpha=\frac{\pi}{4},c=(0,0),a=(1,0),b±​=(−cosα,±sinα),α=4π​,

and take G1={c,a}G_1=\{c,a\}G1​={c,a}, G2={c,b+,b−}G_2=\{c,b_+,b_-\}G2​={c,b+​,b−​}.

All three distances from ccc to a,b+,b−a,b_+,b_-a,b+​,b−​ are 111. The remaining distances are ∥b+−b−∥=2\|b_+-b_-\|=\sqrt2∥b+​−b−​∥=2​ and

∥a−b±∥=2+2.\|a-b_\pm\|=\sqrt{2+\sqrt2}.∥a−b±​∥=2+2​​.

Thus the configuration is unit-separated, has no unit triangle, and has exactly two diametral pairs, both cross-grain.

Rotate aaa about ccc by ϕ\phiϕ. The two squared diametral distances become

f±(ϕ)=2+2cos⁡(ϕ±α).f_\pm(\phi)=2+2\cos(\phi\pm\alpha).f±​(ϕ)=2+2cos(ϕ±α).

Although both have negative second derivative at zero,

f±′′(0)=−2cos⁡α<0,f_\pm''(0)=-2\cos\alpha<0,f±′′​(0)=−2cosα<0,

their first derivatives have opposite signs. Consequently

max⁡(f+(ϕ),f−(ϕ))=2+2cos⁡α+2sin⁡α∣ϕ∣+O(ϕ2),\max(f_+(\phi),f_-(\phi)) = 2+2\cos\alpha+2\sin\alpha\,|\phi|+O(\phi^2),max(f+​(ϕ),f−​(ϕ))=2+2cosα+2sinα∣ϕ∣+O(ϕ2),

which increases for either sign of small nonzero ϕ\phiϕ.

So a claim that “all diametral distances have negative second derivative, hence rotation improves the diameter” is false unless their first derivatives are also controlled. This four-site arrangement is not claimed to be globally optimal; it is a counterexample to that local deduction.

## 6. Further false steps ruled out

The following distinctions are important for a referee evaluation.

| Suspected implication | Assessment |
| --- | --- |
| A positive equilibrium stress makes the second-order form nonnegative in every direction | False. Only the critical cone matters, and one must generally maximize over stresses. |
| Every infinitesimal contact flex yields an improving motion | False. A flex may yield merely an equal-diameter family, or be blocked at higher order. |

### Why a purely topological defect theorem cannot finish the job

There are two fundamentally different notions of defect:

1. A geometric or elastic defect, such as positive overlap deficit, angle excess, or departure from regular bond lengths.
2. An exact contact defect, such as a missing unit edge in an otherwise triangular six-neighbor framework.

The first has continuously variable magnitude. The second is binary.

The strained-rhombus example contains a positive density of missing exact unit contacts, while its total geometric excess can be made arbitrarily small relative to the number of sites.

There is therefore no uniform estimate of the form

δp≥c1{missing exact contact at p}(c>0).\delta_p\ge c\, \mathbf1_{\{\text{missing exact contact at }p\}} \qquad(c>0).δp​≥c1{missing exact contact at p}​(c>0).

Similarly, topological Burgers charge can vanish identically when the missing exact contacts arise from a compatible strain.

This identifies the gap in the proposed strategy: exact contact loss is not automatically accompanied by a positive quantized dislocation charge.

A theorem using global optimality could potentially overcome the gap, but it would have to derive a new rigidity or boundary-pinning condition rather than rely solely on quantized grain defects.

## 10. What an endpoint-closing theorem would need to establish

The strongest concrete research direction emerging from this analysis is to combine the exact stress tensor (8.4) with the near-hexagonal original-site estimates.

A useful candidate statement would be:

Proposed boundary-pinning theorem — unproved.

For all sufficiently large nnn, let PPP be a global minimum-diameter unit-separated planar configuration whose original sites satisfy the established near-hexagonal density and boundary estimates. Then no triangle-free unit-contact graph on PPP admits the nonnegative diameter/contact equilibrium (8.1)–(8.4).

This would immediately solve Erdős #99, because every global optimizer admits that equilibrium.

But no proof is obtained here, and the present results do not establish the proposed statement.

There are two distinct barriers.

First, a rhombic contact framework with four contacts per bulk site can be close to triangular packing density while having no bulk Burgers defects.

Second, the diameter stresses in (8.4) are distributed over exact diametral pairs, whose geometry and multiplicities are not determined by Oler's inequality or the integrated Voronoi defect.

The supplied theorem that every local diameter minimum with D>1D>1D>1 has at least two diametral pairs is consistent with this analysis. In particular, replacing the stress system by an argument requiring a unique diametral pair would discard all actual local minimizers in that range.

One potential route is to prove that the angular or directional structure of the diameter stresses cannot pin a triangle-free rhombic bulk efficiently enough at the outer boundary. Such a result would have to be sharp on the exact feasible boundary, not merely asymptotically sharp in packing density.

For the selected JJJ-maximizer, Proposition 4 additionally places a diametral endpoint in every contact component. Equations (10)–(11) show that positive contact stresses must ultimately be balanced by diametral stresses.

These results suggest two precise possible routes to completion.

The stress-support route would prove that every sufficiently large triangle-free global optimizer requires more positive-stress contact edges than planar triangle-free geometry permits, or would establish that all permissible stress supports have a diameter-decreasing deformation. The existing lower bound on the full contact degree is insufficient: zero-stress contacts must be distinguished from positive-stress contacts.

The boundary-pinning route would identify geometric incompatibility between an almost rhombic interior and the actual diametral endpoints of an unrestricted global optimizer. Proposition 6 gives a simple exact instance for two fixed contact directions. An extension to variable-direction rhombus tilings would have to account for train-track deformation modes and all active diameter constraints.

Either route must produce a strict exact-optimality obstruction. The rhombic construction demonstrates why an argument relying only on a strictly positive, but arbitrarily small, local distortion cannot suffice.

### Geometry verdict

The simultaneous construction is compatible. It is not merely a collection of twelve individually feasible modifications.

The critical invariant is that each inserted packet is separated from all original sites except those removed by its own deletion interval, while all distinct inserted packets are mutually unit-separated.

Further deletions made by other packets can only make a valid configuration sparser. Overlapping deletion labels can only make the sum of individual deletion counts an overestimate, which is harmless for the lower population bound.

## 8. Remaining gap to Erdős #99

The principal logical gap lies entirely after the population theorem.

To force an exact original unit triangle, one must obtain information about the unit-contact graph of the original globally minimizing configuration.

The proved inequality (7) is independent of that graph.

In particular, it gives no lower bound for the number of unit contacts and does not establish exact equality in any original-site Voronoi or lens defect.

Even the presence of n−O(D)n-O(D)n−O(D) approximately hexagonal neighborhoods is insufficient for exact unit triangles.

### A direct obstruction to approximate-contact reasoning

Consider a finite triangular-lattice disk packing with horizontal unit contacts. Apply the anisotropic transformation

Tε(x,y)=(x,(1+ε)y),ε>0.T_\varepsilon(x,y)=(x,(1+\varepsilon)y), \qquad \varepsilon>0.Tε​(x,y)=(x,(1+ε)y),ε>0.

Every pairwise distance weakly increases, so the transformed configuration remains unit-separated.

An originally unit-distance pair remains at unit distance only if its vertical displacement was zero. Consequently, every surviving unit contact is horizontal.

A unit equilateral triangle cannot have all three edges horizontal.

Thus the transformed finite set is exactly triangle-free, while its diameter increases by at most a factor 1+ε1+\varepsilon1+ε.

Since ε\varepsilonε can be arbitrarily small, geometric closeness to triangular-lattice density does not force exact contacts.

The transformation does not preserve global optimality. That is precisely why it does not constitute a counterexample to Erdős #99.

## 2. Original priority: Erdős's 1994 statement

The strongest historical attribution is to Paul Erdős's own paper:

P. Erdős, “Some problems in number theory, combinatorics and combinatorial geometry,” Mathematica Pannonica 5 (1994), no. 2, 261–269, §3.2, p. 268.

I inspected page 268 directly. Erdős formulates the minimum-diameter problem and conjectures that every sufficiently large minimizer contains an equilateral triangle with sides of length 111. He also explicitly distinguishes this conjecture from the expectation that sufficiently large optimal configurations are not themselves triangular-lattice subsets.

The historical record establishes three important priority facts:

- The exact unit-triangle conjecture was explicitly posed by Erdős no later than 1994.
- Erdős attributed doubts about its truth to B. H. Sendov and M. Simonovits, not an existing disproof.
- His offered prizes were $100 for a counterexample for infinitely many nnn and $50 for a proof.

This primary statement also creates a useful distinction: proving that global minimizers are eventually nonlattice is compatible with Erdős's triangle conjecture. It does not refute it.

## 7. Which proposed lemmas survive these tests?

| Proposed implication | Assessment |
| --- | --- |
| Three or more unit contacts at an interior original point force a unit triangle | False: six-point global wheel |
| Five unit contacts at an interior point of a global optimizer force a triangle | False: same wheel |
| Every interior original point of every global optimizer has a unit contact | False as a universal finite-nnn statement: eight-point example |
| Local diameter minimality plus exact contact richness forces a unit triangle | False: the constructed infinite family |
| Asymptotic optimality plus local minimality plus four unit contacts at almost every site forces a triangle | False: the same family |
| Every sufficiently large unrestricted global optimizer contains a unit triangle | Not resolved |
| Every sufficiently large global optimizer has a prescribed interior contact degree | Not resolved by these examples |
| A specifically chosen JJJ-maximizing global representative satisfies the stated two-contact condition | Not contradicted |
| Exact equality in the stated six-facet Voronoi-cell theorem forces unit neighbors | Not contradicted |

The infinite construction is particularly relevant to attempts to pass from a high density of almost-hexagonal local structure to exact unit equilateral triangles. It shows that local minimization of diameter can coexist with asymptotically optimal packing density and an abundance of exact unit contacts while retaining no exact unit triangles.

It does not demonstrate that the unrestricted global endpoint has the same property.
